title: Fingering is a plan
summary: Write fingerings into the hard bar, test two different plans, and keep the one that actually works.
materials: the piece from your teacher, with a pencil

figure.alt: A one-octave keyboard from middle C, five neighbouring keys highlighted as an example hard bar. Two different fingering plans, one set of fingers and then another, are written in and tried on the same keys before one is kept.

steps.title: Fingering is a plan
steps.body:
A fingering is a plan for the hand, decided before the hard bar gets fast, not discovered while it is being sight-read at speed. Two different plans can play the exact same notes; one of them will feel wrong every time.

1. Find the hard bar.
2. Write in pencil the fingering your teacher gave, small numbers under the notes, or invent one if there is none.
3. Try a second plan with different fingers, and write it above the first in a different mark.
4. Play both plans slowly, several times each, paying attention to which one avoids awkward crossings.
5. Keep the plan that works, and cross out the other one so your eye is not confused later.

A good fingering plan turns a hard bar into a bar your hand knows what to do with, before a single note goes fast.

steps.title: Four sittings
steps.body: Fifteen minutes each. Tick a sitting when it is done. Days do not matter; sittings do.
checklist: Sitting 1: write in the first fingering plan, play it slowly five times
Sitting 2: write in a second plan for the same bar, play it slowly five times
Sitting 3: compare both plans, keep the better one, cross out the other
Sitting 4: the whole piece with the kept fingering, then once as if recording
An old piece played once, noticing its fingering without changing anything

steps.title: Record this week's version
steps.prompt: Say the name of the piece, then play it once through, hands in the frame.

extras.title: Two plans for one leap
extras.body:
1. Find a jump in the piece where one hand moves suddenly to a far-away key.
2. Play the jump with your first idea for fingering, slowly, five times.
3. Play the same jump using the finger you would use last, instead, five times.
4. Time yourself, roughly, landing the jump cleanly with each plan.

What to notice: the plan that feels most awkward at first is sometimes the one that lands cleanest at speed.
